facts.statement: The researchers used a randomized, blinded experiment to test if the sleep loss from daylight saving time changes how likely people are to click phishing links.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The study involved 11,218 employees who were split into two groups: one received the email on the Monday after the daylight saving time change, and the other received it one week earlier.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Participants who received the email after the sleep loss were about 13 percent more likely to click a suspicious link than those who received it earlier, but their rates of opening the email or marking it as spam did not change.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The authors conclude that small, sudden amounts of lost sleep can significantly increase the risk of cognitive errors in real-world situations.
facts.subject: humans
